title: Rama Speaks First
hookLine: the night before his coronation, Ayodhya lists why it loves Rama: he speaks first, with a smile; in Hinduism, dharma lives in daily speech
carry: dharma lives in who speaks first

cards: Ayodhya, the night before a coronation. King Dasharatha has grown old, and he's decided his eldest son Rama will be crowned prince in the morning. He calls the assembly and asks them: is this the right choice?
The answer comes back as a list. Not battles won, not bows bent. Most of what the people love about Rama is how he treats them.

teach.h: RAMA SPEAKS FIRST, WITH A SMILE
teach.b: This is the opening of the Ayodhya book of Valmiki's Ramayana, and the poet lingers on Rama's character. He speaks first, with a smile. He doesn't answer harsh words with harsh words.

One kindness done for him, and he's content; a hundred wrongs, and he doesn't keep count. When he comes home, he asks the townspeople about their children, their household fires, their work, the way a father would.
It's part of why Rama is called maryada purushottama, the best of people, within the bounds of dharma.
And notice where his dharma shows first: not on a battlefield, but in a greeting. Here's the teaching. In Hinduism, dharma, right living, isn't only the big choices.
It lives in daily conduct, very much in speech. Ayurveda builds this into the daily routine itself.
The Ashtanga Hridaya calls it sadvritta, good conduct, and puts it in the same chapter as brushing your teeth. Every action, it says, is aimed at happiness, and there's no happiness without dharma.

Then it gets specific: speak at the right time, helpfully, in measure, pleasantly, and be the first to speak, with a friendly face. Rama's habit, written into a health manual. Today, that's a hard one.

When there's been distance with someone, the easy move is to wait and see whether they'll be warm first. The Hindu answer, from the epic to the physicians, is to go first. Not grovelling, not pretending nothing happened.
Just the first namaste, the first hello, with a real face behind it.

how: Hindus hold up Rama as the model of dharma in daily conduct, and Ayurvedic texts include sadvritta, good conduct, in the daily routine: timely, kind speech and being the first to greet.

o: the day's conduct, kind speech and greeting included
the fixed times for meals and sleep, nothing more
a list of chores done in strict order each day

games.q: dharma in a greeting — tap the pairs.
p: the best of people, within dharma

s: Valmiki describes Rama as one who speaks first, with a smile
kind even to harsh words, and quick to let wrongs go.
in Hinduism, dharma is only about big life choices
it lives in daily conduct too, and Ayurveda puts good conduct inside the daily routine.
the Ashtanga Hridaya's speech advice is just 'be nice'
it's specific: the right time, helpful, measured, pleasant, and greet first.

games.q: a friend you drifted from sits down near you. neither of you speaks. what's Rama's way?
o: wait to see what mood they're in.
speak first, with a friendly face.
games.why: Valmiki's Rama speaks first, with a smile, and the Ashtanga Hridaya says the same: be the first to speak, with a pleasant face.

practice: Bring to mind someone you'll likely see soon, someone you've been waiting on to be warm first. Fold your hands at your chest and see yourself greeting them first: namaste, or a simple hi, with a real face, not a forced one.
Notice what happens in the body as you picture it. Then rest in the breath; if you pray, hold that person in your prayer for a moment.

wordCard.voice: The daily routine. In the Ashtanga Hridaya it includes sadvritta, good conduct: speak helpfully, in measure, and be the first to greet, the way Rama did.

orig.note: Sanskrit sadvritta: good conduct, the ethical part of Ayurveda's daily routine.

carryVoice: Your line: dharma lives in who speaks first. Rama's way, kept daily, at every hello. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda, opening cantos (Rama's virtues as Dasharatha and the assembly weigh his coronation: he speaks first, with a smile; does not answer harsh words; is pleased by one kindness and forgets a hundred wrongs; asks after the townspeople's children, fires and work)
Ashtanga Hridaya, Sutrasthana 2.20 (all activities of beings are for happiness; there is no happiness without dharma; so be devoted to dharma)
Ashtanga Hridaya, Sutrasthana 2.26 (speak at the right time, beneficial, measured, consistent and pleasant words; be the first to speak, with a pleasant face)
Charaka Samhita, Sutrasthana 8 (sadvritta, rules of good conduct)
